A scalar is completely specified by its magnitude (a number with a unit) alone, while a vector needs both a magnitude and a direction and obeys the laws of vector addition.
Scalars: speed, work done, power, energy, electric charge.
Vectors: velocity, displacement, force, acceleration, angular velocity.

Average velocity: the displacement of the object during a time interval divided by that time interval. If \(\vec{x}_1\) and \(\vec{x}_2\) are the position vectors of the object at times \(t_1\) and \(t_2\), then
\(\vec{v}_{av} = \frac{\vec{x}_2 - \vec{x}_1}{t_2 - t_1}\)
Its direction is along the displacement \(\vec{x}_2 - \vec{x}_1\).
Instantaneous velocity: the velocity of the object at a given instant of time \(t\). It is the limiting value of the average velocity taken over a small time interval \(\Delta t\) around \(t\), as \(\Delta t\) goes to zero.
\(\vec{v} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\left(\frac{\Delta \vec{x}}{\Delta t}\right) = \frac{d\vec{x}}{dt}\)
Graphically it is the slope of the tangent to the position-time curve at that instant.
The two are the same for uniform motion, i.e. when the object moves with constant velocity (zero acceleration) along a straight line. The position-time graph is then a straight line whose slope is the same everywhere, so the average velocity over every interval equals the instantaneous velocity at every instant.

When a body starts with zero velocity at a certain height above the ground and falls under the influence of the gravity of the Earth alone, it is said to be in free fall.
The only other force that acts on it is that of air resistance or friction; for displacements of a few metres this force is too small and can be neglected. The acceleration of the body is then the acceleration due to gravity \(g\), which is along the vertical direction and can be taken to be constant over distances small compared with the radius of the Earth. Thus the velocity and the acceleration are both along the vertical and free fall is a uniform rectilinear motion with uniform acceleration \(g\).

Here \(x = f(t)\) gives the position of the object as a function of time.
Instantaneous velocity is the limiting value of the average velocity as the time interval goes to zero, i.e. the first derivative of the position with respect to time:
\(v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\left(\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\right) = \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left[f(t)\right]\)
Instantaneous acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time, i.e. the second derivative of the position with respect to time:
\(a = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\left(\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\right) = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = \frac{d^2}{dt^2}\left[f(t)\right]\)

Let a particle move in the \(xy\) plane with uniform acceleration \(\vec{a}\). Let its velocity be \(\vec{u}\) at \(t = 0\) and \(\vec{v}\) at time \(t\), and let \(\vec{s}\) be its displacement in that time.
First equation: as the acceleration is constant, the average acceleration and the instantaneous acceleration are equal, so by the definition of acceleration
\(\vec{a} = \frac{\vec{v} - \vec{u}}{t - 0}\)
\(\therefore \vec{v} = \vec{u} + \vec{a}\,t\)
Second equation: since the acceleration is constant the velocity changes linearly with time, so the average velocity over the interval is
\(\vec{v}_{av} = \frac{\vec{u} + \vec{v}}{2}\)
\(\therefore \vec{s} = \vec{v}_{av}\,t = \left(\frac{\vec{u} + \vec{v}}{2}\right)t = \left(\frac{\vec{u} + \vec{u} + \vec{a}t}{2}\right)t\)
\(\therefore \vec{s} = \vec{u}\,t + \frac{1}{2}\vec{a}\,t^2\)
Resolution into two perpendicular motions: write each vector in terms of its components along the mutually perpendicular unit vectors \(\hat{i}\) and \(\hat{j}\):
\(\vec{u} = u_x\hat{i} + u_y\hat{j}\), \(\vec{v} = v_x\hat{i} + v_y\hat{j}\), \(\vec{a} = a_x\hat{i} + a_y\hat{j}\), \(\vec{s} = s_x\hat{i} + s_y\hat{j}\)
Substituting these in the two vector equations and equating the coefficients of \(\hat{i}\) and of \(\hat{j}\) separately (which is permitted because \(\hat{i}\) and \(\hat{j}\) are mutually perpendicular and hence independent), we get the scalar equations
\(v_x = u_x + a_x t\) and \(v_y = u_y + a_y t\)
\(s_x = u_x t + \frac{1}{2}a_x t^2\) and \(s_y = u_y t + \frac{1}{2}a_y t^2\)
The first pair involves only the \(x\) components of displacement, velocity and acceleration, and the second pair involves only the \(y\) components. No equation of one set contains a quantity belonging to the other set, so the two sets are independent of each other and can be solved separately.
Hence the motion along the \(x\) direction is completely controlled by \(u_x\) and \(a_x\), and that along the \(y\) direction is completely controlled by \(u_y\) and \(a_y\). Motion in a plane can therefore be resolved into two independent rectilinear motions in two mutually perpendicular directions.

Consider an object moving along a straight line with uniform acceleration \(a\). Let its position be \(x = 0\) at \(t = 0\), its velocity be \(u\) at \(t = 0\) and \(v\) at time \(t\). Since the acceleration is uniform, the velocity-time graph is the straight line \(AB\), with the intercept \(OA = u\) and the ordinate \(BD = v\) at time \(t\). Drop \(AC\) parallel to the time axis and \(BD\) perpendicular to it, so that \(OACD\) is a rectangle and \(ABC\) is a triangle.
First equation: the acceleration is the slope of the line \(AB\).
\(a = \frac{v - u}{t - 0} = \frac{v - u}{t}\)
\(\therefore v = u + at\)
Second equation: the area under the velocity-time graph between two instants gives the displacement in that interval. Here
\(s = \text{area of quadrilateral } OABD = \text{area of rectangle } OACD + \text{area of triangle } ABC\)
\(s = ut + \frac{1}{2}(AC)(BC) = ut + \frac{1}{2}(t)(v - u)\)
Using \(v - u = at\),
\(\therefore s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2\)
Third equation: \(OABD\) is a trapezium with parallel sides \(OA = u\) and \(DB = v\) and height \(OD = t\), so its area gives
\(s = \frac{1}{2}(u + v)t\)
From the first equation \(t = \frac{v - u}{a}\). Substituting,
\(s = \frac{1}{2}(u + v)\left(\frac{v - u}{a}\right) = \frac{v^2 - u^2}{2a}\)
\(\therefore v^2 - u^2 = 2as\)
Thus the three equations of motion for uniform acceleration are \(v = u + at\), \(s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2\) and \(v^2 - u^2 = 2as\).

Take the origin at the point of projection, the \(x\) axis along the ground and the \(y\) axis vertically upwards. The projectile is thrown with initial velocity \(\vec{u}\) making an angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal, so
\(u_x = u\cos\theta\), \(u_y = u\sin\theta\)
The acceleration due to gravity acts only vertically downwards, so \(a_x = 0\) and \(a_y = -g\). Hence the horizontal component of velocity stays unchanged while the vertical component changes:
\(v_x = u\cos\theta\), \(v_y = u\sin\theta - gt\)
and the displacements at time \(t\) are
\(s_x = (u\cos\theta)t\), \(s_y = (u\sin\theta)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2\)
At the highest point the vertical component of velocity is zero. If \(t_0\) is the time taken to reach it, then
\(0 = u\sin\theta - gt_0\)
\(\therefore t_0 = \frac{u\sin\theta}{g}\)
The trajectory is symmetrical, so the object takes the same time going up and coming down, and the total time of flight is \(T = 2t_0\).
Range: the horizontal distance covered in time \(T\) is
\(R = u_x T = (u\cos\theta)\left(\frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}\right) = \frac{u^2(2\sin\theta\cos\theta)}{g}\)
\(\therefore R = \frac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}\)
Maximum height: the vertical distance covered in time \(t_0\) is
\(H = (u\sin\theta)t_0 - \frac{1}{2}gt_0^2 = u\sin\theta\left(\frac{u\sin\theta}{g}\right) - \frac{1}{2}g\left(\frac{u\sin\theta}{g}\right)^2\)
\(= \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{g} - \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\)
\(\therefore H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\)
Hence the horizontal range is \(R = \frac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}\) and the maximum height is \(H = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}\).

Let a projectile be thrown from the origin with initial velocity \(\vec{u}\) at an angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal, the \(x\) axis being horizontal and the \(y\) axis vertically upwards. Since \(a_x = 0\) and \(a_y = -g\), the displacements at time \(t\) are
\(x = (u\cos\theta)t\) and \(y = (u\sin\theta)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2\)
The equation of the path is the relation between \(y\) and \(x\), obtained by eliminating \(t\) between these two.
From the first, \(t = \frac{x}{u\cos\theta}\). Substituting in the second,
\(y = (u\sin\theta)\left(\frac{x}{u\cos\theta}\right) - \frac{1}{2}g\left(\frac{x}{u\cos\theta}\right)^2\)
\(\therefore y = (\tan\theta)x - \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{g}{u^2\cos^2\theta}\right)x^2\)
For a given projection \(u\) and \(\theta\) are constants, so putting \(A = \tan\theta\) and \(B = -\frac{g}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}\), this is of the form
\(y = Ax + Bx^2\)
with \(B \neq 0\) (since \(g \neq 0\) and \(\theta \neq 90^\circ\)). This is the equation of a parabola.
Hence the path, i.e. the trajectory of a projectile, is a parabola.

Conical pendulum: in a simple pendulum a mass \(m\) is suspended by a string of length \(l\) and moves along an arc of a vertical circle. If instead the mass revolves in a horizontal circle so that the string makes a constant angle \(\theta\) with the vertical, the string describes a cone whose vertex is the fixed point of support \(O\). Such a mass-string system is called a conical pendulum. In the absence of friction it continues indefinitely once started.
Only two forces act on the bob: its weight \(mg\) vertically downwards, and the force due to the tension in the string directed along the string towards the support. Let this tension be \(F\), and let \(T\) denote the time period of revolution.
Resolve \(F\) into two mutually perpendicular components: \(F\cos\theta\) vertically upwards and \(F\sin\theta\) horizontally, towards the centre \(O'\) of the horizontal circle. The radius of that circle is
\(r = l\sin\theta\)
There is no vertical motion, so the vertical component must balance the weight:
\(F\cos\theta = mg\)
The remaining horizontal component is radial, i.e. directed towards the centre, and it provides the centripetal force:
\(F\sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r}\)
Dividing the second equation by the first,
\(\tan\theta = \frac{F\sin\theta}{F\cos\theta} = \frac{mv^2/r}{mg} = \frac{v^2}{rg}\)
For uniform circular motion \(v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}\), so
\(\tan\theta = \frac{4\pi^2 r^2}{T^2 rg} = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2 g}\)
\(\therefore T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 r}{g\tan\theta}\)
\(\therefore T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r}{g\tan\theta}}\)
Putting \(r = l\sin\theta\),
\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l\sin\theta}{g\tan\theta}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g\sin\theta}}\)
\(\therefore T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l\cos\theta}{g}}\)
This is the required result. Since \(h = l\cos\theta\) is the vertical distance of the horizontal circle below the point of support, it can also be written as \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{h}{g}}\).

[Textbook note: the question asks for a definition of angular VELOCITY, but §3.4.1 of this chapter defines only angular SPEED, a scalar. The model answer supplies the direction of the vector (along the axis, by the right-hand rule), which is standard physics but is NOT stated anywhere in this chapter.]

Angular velocity: for a particle moving along a circle, the angular velocity is the angle described by its radius vector per unit time, \(\omega = \frac{d\theta}{dt}\). It is a vector directed along the axis of rotation, its sense being given by the right hand rule, and its unit is radian per second. During one complete revolution the angle described is \(2\pi\) in time \(T\), so
\(\omega = \frac{\text{angle}}{\text{time}} = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{v}{r}\)
Centripetal force: consider a particle \(P\) of mass \(m\) performing uniform circular motion in the anticlockwise sense along a circle of radius \(r\) with constant angular speed \(\omega\). Choose the \(xy\) plane for the motion with the centre of the circle at the origin \(O\), and let the particle start on the positive \(x\) axis. At time \(t\) the radius vector makes an angle \(\theta = \omega t\) with the \(x\) axis, so its \(x\) and \(y\) components are \(r\cos\theta\) and \(r\sin\theta\):
\(\vec{r} = \left(r\cos\omega t\right)\hat{i} + \left(r\sin\omega t\right)\hat{j}\)
The magnitudes \(r\) and \(\omega\) are constants. Differentiating with respect to time gives the instantaneous velocity:
\(\vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt} = r\left(-\omega\sin\omega t\,\hat{i} + \omega\cos\omega t\,\hat{j}\right) = r\omega\left(-\sin\omega t\,\hat{i} + \cos\omega t\,\hat{j}\right)\)
Differentiating once more gives the instantaneous acceleration:
\(\vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = r\omega\left(-\omega\cos\omega t\,\hat{i} - \omega\sin\omega t\,\hat{j}\right)\)
\(= -\omega^2\left(r\cos\omega t\,\hat{i} + r\sin\omega t\,\hat{j}\right)\)
\(\therefore \vec{a} = -\omega^2\vec{r}\)
The minus sign shows that the acceleration is opposite in direction to \(\vec{r}\), i.e. it is directed towards the centre of the circle; this is the centripetal acceleration. By Newton's second law the force producing it is along the same direction, and is
\(\vec{F} = m\vec{a} = -m\omega^2\vec{r}\)
Hence the centripetal force on a particle performing uniform circular motion is \(-m\omega^2\vec{r}\), its magnitude being \(F = m\omega^2 r = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega v\).
